papers.title: TSAI-MetaFraud: A Benchmark Dataset for Financial Fraud Transaction and Behavioral Risk Detection in Metaverse Ecosystems
papers.authors: Refat Ishrak Hemel, Ehsan Hallaji, Roozbeh Razavi-Far
papers.abstract: The emergence of metaverse platforms has created virtual economies that introduce new challenges related to fraud, bot activity, and illicit financial behavior. Despite growing interest in trustworthy metaverse analytics, existing datasets typically focus on user behavior, authentication, or financial transactions in isolation, limiting the development and reproducible evaluation of multimodal fraud detection methods. To address this gap, we present TSAI-MetaFraud, a multimodal, multi-task benchmark dataset for fraud analytics in virtual economies. TSAI-MetaFraud integrates behavioral, transactional, and graph-structured information while incorporating realistic fraud and automated bot scenarios. We define benchmark tasks including transaction fraud detection, cross-modal node classification, temporal link prediction, and weakly supervised fraud detection, and provide baseline evaluations using machine learning models and graph neural networks. By jointly capturing behavioral activity, financial interactions, and relational structure within a unified virtual economy, TSAI-MetaFraud provides a benchmark for advancing multimodal learning, graph mining, fraud analytics, and trustworthy AI in emerging metaverse ecosystems.
takeaways: Introduces TSAI-MetaFraud, a multimodal, multi-task benchmark dataset for fraud analytics in metaverse virtual economies, combining behavioral, transactional, and graph-structured data.

Defines benchmark tasks for transaction fraud detection, cross-modal node classification, temporal link prediction, and weakly supervised fraud detection, with baseline evaluations using machine learning models and graph neural networks.
Provides a reproducible testbed for developing and comparing multimodal fraud detection, graph mining, and trustworthy AI methods in emerging metaverse ecosystems.
actionItems: Review the TSAI-MetaFraud benchmark scope and task definitions to determine which of the four benchmark tasks and which data modalities align with your current fraud analytics pipeline.

Assess whether your intended metaverse fraud use case can realistically match the dataset's multimodal, graph-structured setting and whether the dataset's low applicability/reproducibility signals affect adoption.

papers.title: FreyaTTS Technical Report
papers.authors: Ahmet Erdem Pamuk, Ömer Yentür, Ahmet Tunga Bayrak, Yavuz Alp Sencer Öztürk, Mustafa Yavuz
papers.abstract: We introduce Freya-TTS, a compact, tokenizer-free, Turkish-first text-to-speech model designed for highly reliable and efficient conversational synthesis. Freya-TTS is a 183.2M-parameter non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that operates in the frozen continuous latent space of AudioVAE2 (16 kHz encode, 48 kHz decode), allowing the model to focus its capacity on text-to-latent mapping while inheriting high-quality 48 kHz reconstruction. We advance the framework along three key dimensions: (1) rule-free end-to-end modeling from a 92-symbol Turkish character vocabulary without a phonemizer, grapheme-to-phoneme frontend, or discrete speech tokenizer; (2) non-autoregressive parallel denoising, which predicts the entire latent sequence simultaneously over a predicted duration; and (3) a production-oriented two-stage post-training recipe consisting of single-speaker voice locking and short-utterance coverage, improving speaker consistency and robustness on short inputs. On the Freya-TR-Eval benchmark, Freya-TTS achieves a band-matched word error rate (WER) of 8.0% and character error rate (CER) of 3.0%, outperforming substantially larger open-source systems while using a fraction of their parameters. The model achieves a real-time factor of 0.11 on consumer GPUs and runs faster than real time on a laptop CPU, making it well suited for resource-constrained edge deployment. We release the model weights, training and inference code, and evaluation benchmark under the Apache-2.0 license.
takeaways: Freya-TTS is a compact, Turkish-first, tokenizer-free text-to-speech model that uses a 183.2M-parameter non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching DiT in a frozen AudioVAE2 latent space.

The report evaluates Freya-TTS on Freya-TR-Eval, where it reaches 8.0% band-matched WER and 3.0% CER, with a two-stage post-training recipe for single-speaker voice locking and short-utterance coverage.

The model is positioned for efficient deployment: it runs at 0.11 real-time factor on consumer GPUs, faster than real time on a laptop CPU, and the authors release weights, code, and benchmark under Apache-2.0.
actionItems: Review the Freya-TR-Eval benchmark setup and band-matched WER/CER calculation to verify that the reported 8.0% WER and 3.0% CER are directly comparable across the released evaluation conditions.

Run an ablation or replication focused on the two-stage post-training recipe, comparing single-speaker voice locking and short-utterance coverage against the base model on speaker consistency, short-input robustness, and WER/CER.
Assess whether the tokenizer-free Turkish-first design and frozen AudioVAE2 latent-space dependency generalize to non-Turkish or broader deployment settings, especially for edge use cases.

papers.title: 4DR360: State Reasoning for Joint 3D Detection and Occupancy Prediction in 4D Radar-Camera Full-Scene Perception
papers.authors: Xiaokai Bai, Lianqing Zheng, Runwei Guan, Songkai Wang, Siyuan Cao, Hui-liang Shen
papers.abstract: Reliable autonomous driving requires full-scene perception that couples foreground objects with dense semantic layout. Recently, 4D millimeter-wave radar has emerged as a robust and affordable sensor, yet its sparse returns make radar-camera fusion necessary for comprehensive scene understanding. Existing radar-camera methods mainly optimize detection, while dual-task systems usually decode boxes and occupancy with limited interaction. To address this gap and advance radar-based multi-task learning, we propose \method, a 4D radar-camera framework for 360$^\circ$ full-scene perception, which models semantic occupancy as a persistent scene state rather than a terminal output. \method{} follows a cross-modal state reasoning paradigm, where the occupancy state is modeled and propagated through stages for coarse-to-fine feature aggregation. Specifically, State-guided BEV Enhancement (SBE) strengthens intra-frame BEV representation, while Doppler-guided Temporal Fusion (DTF) preserves state evidence over longer temporal horizons. Beyond the model, we further extend ManTruckScenes with satellite-map-based generated occupancy labels and pair it with OmniHD-Scenes in a unified cross-dataset detection-and-occupancy protocol. The resulting experiments cover accuracy, robustness, ablation, and efficiency under one radar-camera multi-task evaluation framework. Code and labels will be released upon acceptance.
takeaways: Proposes 4DR360, a 4D radar-camera 360° full-scene perception framework that treats semantic occupancy as a persistent scene state and jointly targets 3D detection and occupancy prediction.

Uses cross-modal state reasoning with State-guided BEV Enhancement for intra-frame feature aggregation and Doppler-guided Temporal Fusion to carry occupancy evidence across time; evaluates on a unified cross-dataset protocol.

Practical implication: aims to improve radar-based autonomous driving perception beyond box detection alone, with added occupancy labels for ManTruckScenes and reported experiments on accuracy, robustness, ablation, and efficiency.
actionItems: Review the cross-modal state reasoning design in 4DR360, focusing on how State-guided BEV Enhancement and Doppler-guided Temporal Fusion are used to propagate semantic occupancy as a persistent scene state.

Run a cross-dataset evaluation that checks both 3D detection and occupancy prediction on the unified ManTruckScenes and OmniHD-Scenes protocol, including accuracy, robustness, ablation, and efficiency comparisons.

Assess whether the added occupancy labels and 360° radar-camera pipeline can be adopted in your driving stack, especially given the need for satellite-map-generated labels and the stated low applicability outside radar-based autonomous driving perception.

papers.title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
papers.authors: Xiangxin Zhao, Han Li, Shuaiting Li, Tianyi Zhao, Earl T. Barr, Federica Sarro, He Ye
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly deployed to autonomously perform software engineering tasks in terminal-based environments, making their reliability a growing concern. Existing empirical studies investigate why coding agents fail, yet they largely treat failure as a final outcome rather than a temporal process, providing limited insight into how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable. We present the first large-scale empirical study of CLI coding-agent failure trajectories, introducing a process-oriented framework that analyzes failure through its onset, evolution, and recovery across execution trajectories. We first collect 3,843 execution trajectories generated by seven frontier models across three coding-agent scaffolds (OpenHands, MiniSWE, and Terminus2) on Terminal-Bench, then carefully filter them to obtain 1,794 complete and valid trajectories for manual annotation (over 63,000 execution steps), from which we derive 14 findings spanning failure occurrence, root causes, recovery, and cross-system consistency. Our findings show that coding-agent failures are predominantly driven by epistemic errors, typically begin within the first few execution steps, and often remain hidden until recovery is no longer possible, suggesting that improving coding-agent reliability requires earlier validation and intervention rather than relying solely on final-outcome evaluation.
takeaways: Introduces a process-oriented framework for CLI coding-agent failures, analyzing failure onset, evolution, and recovery rather than treating failure as only a final outcome.

Studies 3,843 trajectories from seven frontier models across OpenHands, MiniSWE, and Terminus2 on Terminal-Bench, filtering to 1,794 valid trajectories and 63,000+ annotated steps to derive 14 findings.
Shows failures are mainly driven by epistemic errors, usually start in the first few steps, and can stay hidden until recovery is impossible, implying earlier validation and intervention are needed.
actionItems: Review the process-oriented failure framework and the 14 findings to identify which failure onset, evolution, and recovery signals are most relevant for your CLI coding-agent dashboard.

Run a trajectory-level evaluation on Terminal-Bench-style logs that flags early-step epistemic errors and compares whether early validation/intervention reduces unrecoverable failures across OpenHands, MiniSWE, and Terminus2.
Ask whether your adoption workflow can support earlier validation and intervention in terminal-based coding agents, given that failures may remain hidden until recovery is no longer possible.

papers.title: Evolution of Accuracy and Visual-Cognitive Errors in a Decade of Vision-Language AI Models
papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have made remarkable progress in visual reasoning during the last decade. Most evaluations have used simple scenes (MS-COCO) that do not showcase complex human interactions or behaviors, only a handful of non-curated human descriptions as a benchmark, and have not focused on understanding the model's error types. Here, we introduce the Complex Social Behavior (CSB) dataset, containing 100 images depicting complex social interactions/behaviors. We analyze the progression of scene descriptions over a decade (2017-2025) of VLMs (four pre-Multimodal Large Language Models, MLLMs, and five MLLMs). We evaluate the accuracy of the models and 20 human descriptions relative to a gold standard on the CSB dataset and on a sample from MS-COCO. We analyzed five visual-cognitive error types: object detection, recognition, hallucination, scene understanding, and spatial dependence. The CSB dataset showed a more pronounced improvement than MS-COCO in scene description accuracy, with pre-MLLMs achieving much lower accuracy than the bottom-ranked human descriptions and MLLMs attaining accuracies similar to the top-ranked human descriptions. We show that MLLMs have eliminated the gap in scene description accuracy between simpler MS-COCO scenes and scenes depicting complex behaviors (CSB). MLLMs have almost eliminated all error types in our tested datasets, except for occasionally relying on different image regions for scene descriptions than humans do (spatial dependence error). We also show that detection, recognition, and hallucination errors have the highest impact on scene description accuracy. Together, our findings provide a more thorough evaluation of how visual language models have advanced over the last decade.
takeaways: Introduces the Complex Social Behavior (CSB) dataset of 100 images to evaluate VLM scene descriptions on complex human interactions and track 2017–2025 model progress against human descriptions.

Compares four pre-MLLMs, five MLLMs, and 20 human descriptions on CSB and MS-COCO, analyzing accuracy plus five visual-cognitive error types: object detection, recognition, hallucination, scene understanding, and spatial dependence.

Finds MLLMs match top human description accuracy on CSB and largely remove the CSB–MS-COCO gap, suggesting improved evaluation of complex social scenes while spatial dependence remains a residual issue.
actionItems: Review the CSB dataset design and the 2017–2025 model-vs-human comparison setup, including the gold-standard labeling and the two evaluation corpora (CSB and MS-COCO).

Re-run or replicate the accuracy and five error-type analysis on the 100-image CSB set, with special attention to how object detection, recognition, hallucination, scene understanding, and spatial dependence are scored.

Assess whether the remaining spatial dependence error would affect adoption in tasks that require human-like attention to image regions, even when overall description accuracy matches top human descriptions.

papers.title: MedRealMM: A Real-World Multimodal Benchmark for Chinese Online Medical Consultation
papers.authors: Runhan Shi, Quan Zhou, Yuqian Xu, Shuai Yang, Xin Wu, Zitong Zhou, Hui Liu, Bin Cha, Zheming Wang, Liya Li, Wei Wei, Haoyuan Hu, Jun Xu
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in online medical consultation, yet existing benchmarks remain poorly aligned with real clinical practice. Many rely on synthetic conversations or patient simulators, omit patient-uploaded medical images, or evaluate open-ended clinical responses using multiple-choice or lexical-overlap metrics that poorly reflect clinical quality. We introduce \textbf{MedRealMM}, a large-scale benchmark for multimodal online medical consultation built from de-identified patient-doctor interactions collected from a nationwide Chinese internet hospital. MedRealMM uses a Multimodal Clinical Challenge Point (MCCP) extraction framework to identify clinically demanding moments in authentic consultation trajectories and converts each into a standardized next-response generation task while preserving the preceding text-image context. Each instance is paired with a case-specific rubric refined by physicians that rewards clinically desirable behaviors and penalizes unsafe, unsupported, or contradictory responses. The current release contains 5,620 real-world multimodal cases spanning 64 clinical departments. We evaluate 19 general-purpose and medical-specialized LLMs, including text-only and multimodal systems. Our results show that image information is critical for reliable clinical performance and that current frontier models remain below the online physician response. Although some frontier models satisfy as many or more positive clinical criteria than physicians, they trigger more negative criteria, indicating that safety-sensitive error avoidance remains a central bottleneck. MedRealMM offers a realistic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating multimodal medical reasoning in real-world online consultation. The dataset will be publicly available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jdh-algo/MedRealMM.
takeaways: Introduces MedRealMM, a large-scale real-world multimodal benchmark for Chinese online medical consultation built from de-identified doctor-patient interactions and case-specific physician rubrics.

Uses an MCCP extraction framework to turn authentic text-image consultation histories into next-response generation tasks; evaluates 19 general-purpose and medical LLMs on 5,620 cases across 64 departments.
Finds patient-uploaded images are critical and current frontier models still trail physicians, with safety-sensitive negative errors remaining a key bottleneck for deployment.
actionItems: Review MedRealMM’s MCCP next-response setup and physician-refined rubrics to see how closely the benchmark matches your intended multimodal medical consultation evaluation needs.
Run a comparative evaluation on the 5,620-case benchmark with and without patient-uploaded images to quantify how image context changes model performance and negative error rates.
Assess whether the benchmark’s safety-sensitive error profile and Chinese online-hospital setting are appropriate for your deployment target before using results to support adoption decisions.

papers.title: Multimodal Scenario Similarity Search for Autonomous Driving
papers.authors: Tamás Matuszka, András Tamásy, Balázs Szolár
papers.abstract: Large-scale autonomous-driving datasets contain vast numbers of recorded scenarios, creating a need for efficient retrieval methods that can identify situations similar to a given query. Existing approaches typically rely on either visual representations or motion-based descriptions, making it difficult to understand their relative strengths and limitations for scenario retrieval. In this work, we present a multimodal framework for autonomous-driving scenario retrieval that combines visual and trajectory-based representations within a unified retrieval pipeline. We investigate two trajectory-based approaches: Exo-Trajectory, an explicit matching method based on surrounding-agent motion, and ScenarioFormer, a transformer-based representation learned from object trajectories using contrastive learning. We compare these approaches against strong vision-based baselines and analyze their behavior across a diverse set of driving scenarios. Experimental results show that trajectory representations provide strong retrieval performance for motion-centric events such as cut-ins, turning maneuvers, and traffic queueing, while visual embeddings excel when appearance cues are informative. Most importantly, combining visual and trajectory information consistently improves retrieval quality, yielding the best overall performance. These findings demonstrate that appearance and motion capture are complementary notions of scenario similarity and motivate multimodal retrieval systems for autonomous-driving data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation.
takeaways: Proposes a multimodal autonomous-driving scenario retrieval framework that unifies visual and trajectory-based representations to search large-scale recorded driving datasets.

Compares two trajectory methods—Exo-Trajectory and ScenarioFormer—against vision-based baselines, finding trajectory features work best for motion-centric events while visual embeddings help when appearance cues matter; combining both gives the best retrieval quality.
Suggests that appearance and motion are complementary for scenario similarity, supporting multimodal tools for data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation.
actionItems: Review the multimodal retrieval pipeline design and the reported comparison between Exo-Trajectory, ScenarioFormer, and vision-based baselines to map which representation is used for motion-centric versus appearance-centric scenario search.

Run an evaluation that reproduces the retrieval comparison on driving scenarios, checking whether combining visual and trajectory information consistently improves quality over single-modality baselines across cut-ins, turning maneuvers, and traffic queueing cases.

Ask whether the multimodal scenario similarity approach is practical for data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation in your setting, given the paper’s low applicability and low reproducibility signals.

papers.title: Letting the Data Speak: Extracting Keywords from Crowdsourced Collections with AI
papers.authors: Miguel Arana-Catania, Catherine Conisbee, Matthew Kidd
papers.abstract: Identifying and assigning keywords at scale is a technical, practical, and ethical challenge for crowdsourced collections. This article reports the findings of the "Extracting Keywords from Crowdsourced Collections" project, which used the Their Finest Hour Online Archive, a crowdsourced Second World War digital collection hosted by the University of Oxford, as a case study. The project evaluated three Natural Language Processing approaches to automate keyword extraction: Named Entity Recognition, Keyword Extraction, and Topic Modelling. It tested these approaches across a range of artificial intelligence techniques, from traditional statistical methods to modern GenAI neural networks. Our quantitative and qualitative findings indicate that Natural Language Processing approaches offer real potential for keyword extraction at scale in crowdsourced collections, but that no single method offers a complete solution and that model choice significantly shapes results. We argue that in crowdsourced collections, where metadata is the direct product of engagement with living contributors, automated keyword extraction raises distinct stewardship responsibilities that must be addressed alongside technical performance. Open-weight, extractive models emerge from our evaluation as best placed to support responsible deployment, while generative AI, despite its abstractive potential, introduces accountability risks that anyone managing crowdsourced collections should weigh carefully.
takeaways: Case study of a University of Oxford crowdsourced WWII archive shows NLP can help extract keywords at scale, but no single method fully solves the problem and model choice materially changes results.

The project compared three approaches—Named Entity Recognition, Keyword Extraction, and Topic Modelling—across methods from traditional statistical techniques to GenAI neural networks, using quantitative and qualitative evaluation.

Practical takeaway: open-weight, extractive models are presented as the safest option for responsible deployment, while generative AI may improve abstraction but raises accountability and stewardship risks for crowdsourced collections.
actionItems: Review the full methodology and evaluation criteria used to compare Named Entity Recognition, keyword extraction, and topic modelling on the Their Finest Hour Online Archive case study, with attention to how model choice changed results.

Plan a follow-up benchmark that reproduces the three approaches across both traditional statistical methods and GenAI neural networks, using quantitative and qualitative measures to compare keyword quality at scale.

Ask whether a crowdsourced collection can support deployment of open-weight extractive models without creating stewardship or accountability issues for contributor-generated metadata, especially if generative AI is considered.
